claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations with temperature ramps can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo thermal instability at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
The lower thermal stability of smaller nanoparticles is caused by their higher surface-to-volume ratio.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio promotes enhanced surface diffusion and earlier structural transformation.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a near-equiatomic composition.
The initial nanoparticles have minimal defects and surface disorder.
Nanoparticle sizes from below 10 nm to 30 nm are suitable for testing the proposed size dependence.
The simulations require interatomic potentials that capture multicomponent interactions.
Heating can produce pronounced atomic diffusion in quinary high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Heating can induce phase separation at the surface of quinary high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles contain a larger fraction of surface atoms.
Elevated temperature promotes diffusion-driven structural and chemical rearrangement in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Enhanced diffusion in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles causes earlier thermal instability or melting.
Nanoparticle size and thermal stability have a clear inverse relationship.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles exhibit surface reconstruction or melting at lower temperatures than larger counterparts.
Interatomic-potential limitations and MD timescales may shift the predicted instability onset temperatures relative to experiment.
